key_concept: Each atrioventricular opening of the human heart has its own valve: the tricuspid valve guards the right atrioventricular opening and the bicuspid (mitral) valve guards the left one.
steps: The human heart has four chambers. On each side, the atrium opens into the ventricle below it through an atrioventricular (AV) aperture.
The right AV opening, between the right atrium and the right ventricle, is guarded by a valve made of three muscular flaps (cusps). This is the tricuspid valve.
The left AV opening, between the left atrium and the left ventricle, is guarded by a valve with two cusps. This is the bicuspid, or mitral, valve.
Semilunar valves sit at the openings of the pulmonary artery and the aorta, which arise from the right and left ventricles respectively.
All these valves allow blood to flow in one direction only, from atria to ventricles and from ventricles into the arteries, and prevent backflow.
Hence the right atrium–right ventricle opening is guarded by the tricuspid valve, matching the official answer (2).
why_not_others: The bicuspid (mitral) valve guards the left AV opening, not the right one. Semilunar valves guard the exits of the ventricles into the pulmonary artery and aorta. The SA node is the pacemaker tissue in the right atrial wall and is not a valve.
common_trap: Students often swap bicuspid and tricuspid, putting the bicuspid valve on the right side.
time_saving_tip: Remember 'Try before you Buy': Tricuspid is on the Right (the 'R' in tRi), and Bicuspid/mitral is on the left.
